newsitem.title: USA: Drug stalls bone deterioration in breast cancer.
newsitem.headline: Drug stalls bone deterioration in breast cancer.

text.p: A drug that hobbles the body's natural ability to dissolve bone can help women with advanced breast cancer whose bones have been worn painfully thin by the disease, according to an international study.

A team led by Dr. Gabriel Hortobagyi of the University of Texas M.D. Anderson Cancer Center found that among women whose breast tumors had spread and were eating away at their bones, those who received the drug pamidronate, sold under the brand name Aredia by Ciba-Geigy, lived longer without developing fractures or needing bone radiation to relieve pain.

For example, the average time for the first bone-related complications to appear was 13 months for women who received monthly infusions of pamidronate, versus seven months in the placebo group. The pamidronate group also experienced reductions in bone pain and the need for pain medicine.
The test results from 97 medical centers in the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand were published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

Breast cancer patients experience an "intense amount of pain and suffering" when the tumor spreads to their bones, Hortobagyi said. "When given along with chemotherapy, this drug provides significant protection against skeletal complications, and eases the patient's pain, offering a better quality of life."

In a healthy body, bone is constantly being remodeled due to a delicate balance between cells that build new bone and cells that destroy unwanted bone. Bone problems are a common complication for women with advanced breast cancer because cancer seems to stimulate the cells that eat away at bone.
About 184,000 women in the United States are diagnosed with breast cancer each year. Nearly 100,000 were living with tumors that have spread to their bones, Hortobagyi said.
Doctors usually treat the problem with chemotherapy and hormones but that can only delay the pain, stiffness and immobility that come after the tumor has spread.

Hortobagyi's team decided to test pamidronate because it belongs to a class of drugs that inhibits the bone destruction process. The researchers gave the drug to 185 volunteers while 195 others received a placebo.

The pamidronate recipients reported significantly less pain after three months of treatments, while "the patients in the placebo group had progressive worsening of bone pain," the researchers concluded in the Journal.
It took six months of therapy to produce a significant difference, "but the effects of pamidronate became more evident with successive treatments," the researchers said.
The drug did not help the cancer patients live longer.

Dr. Pierre Delmas of Edouard Herroit Hospital in Lyon, France, said the new findings raise the question of whether similar drugs, known collectively as bisphosphonates, can help people with other cancers that have spread to the bone.
